posts.first: My first trailer was a rusted two-horse bumper pull I bought for eight hundred dollars. It hauled me to every show for eleven years. I checked the floor with a screwdriver before every trip and said a short prayer at the hitch. I miss it more than I'd admit to a salesman.
posts.caption: The soft spot in our old trailer floor has finally become something we can't ignore, so we drove forty minutes to a dealer lot on Saturday. The salesman had a clipboard and a great deal of confidence. He opened the divider, knocked on the wall, and told us the trailer fit two horses comfortably. I walked my draft mare up the ramp to check for myself. She stepped in, stopped, and stood with her nose against the front wall and her tail against the back gate. It took her eleven seconds to give her opinion. The salesman wrote something down. We're still shopping.

posts.first: I started the folder the week I brought her home, with a manila envelope and a stapler borrowed from the feed store counter. It became a binder, then a box. I can find any vet record in under a minute. I couldn't tell you where I put my car title.
posts.caption: I keep a folder for her on the kitchen shelf, and it's thicker than the one for the house. It holds registration papers, vet records, a Coggins test that expires in March, farrier notes, and four years of show entries she did not win. Last night my husband sat down and read every page. I was braced for a speech. He closed the cover, slid it back across the table, and put his boots on. Ten minutes later he was out at the barn checking her water. She was already waiting at the stall door.

posts.quote: The woman at the feed store knows my horse's name, birthday and favorite treat. She calls me 'the one with the truck.'
posts.first: I've bought grain at the same counter for sixteen years. I've gone from one horse to three and from a hatchback to a used truck, and she's remarked on none of it. Last month she asked if my gelding's cough had cleared up. It had. I stood there longer than I needed to.

posts.first: The chair is green, it folds, and I bought it for six dollars at a yard sale for guests. Nobody else has ever sat in it. He keeps it at the end of the aisle with a thermos and a wool blanket, and I've stopped moving it back.
posts.caption: The old gelding turned twenty-seven in October, and we marked it the way he prefers, which is not at all. He got his usual scoop, a carrot cut into coins, and a long scratch under the forelock. Then my husband stood at the stall door with his coffee and told him about the weather for twenty minutes. The horse blinked slowly through all of it. I think he had already heard the forecast. I didn't interrupt either of them. It rained the next day, and neither of them mentioned it.

posts.first: The string lights were my husband's idea after the power went out for two days last January. They run off a battery pack now, which is the most useful thing anyone has ever bought for this barn. She likes the warm yellow. I like not walking to the water buckets in the dark.
posts.caption: By three-thirty the barn smells like warm beet pulp and wet wool, which is how I know winter has officially started. I soak the pulp in the big blue bucket before lunch and carry it down the aisle with both hands. Every head comes over its stall door at once. Except hers. She's already lying in the straw with her back legs tucked, watching the dusk come in through the window like a show she paid for. I leave her bucket by the door and turn on the string lights. She'll get up when she's ready.

posts.first: I bought Pudding at a small livestock auction for sixty dollars because he looked at me like I owed him something. That was seven years ago. I've been paying it off ever since, mostly in carrots. Nobody has ever offered to buy him back, which is just as well, because the answer would be no.
posts.caption: Pudding makes his rounds at ten every morning. He stops at each stall door, waits until the horse inside looks at him, and then moves on to the next. The barn manager says he's inspecting. The boarders say he's taking attendance. Last week he skipped the new mare's stall, walked three steps, turned around, and stood there until she came over to the door. Then he went back to his hay like nothing had happened. I stopped asking what his job is. The grain bill suggests he's on payroll.
